bib.title: Financial Services (Chapter 9, The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 2nd ed.)

question: How should a retail bank's accounts, households, customers and heterogeneous products be modelled dimensionally?
contributions: Dimension triage to avoid too few dimensions
Household dimension and account-to-customer bridge table
Multiple minidimensions in one fact table with value banding
Band definition table for arbitrary value-band reporting
Point-in-time balances from a transaction fact table
Core and custom schemas for heterogeneous products

results.claim: A daily balance snapshot for a 10 million account bank would be about 3.65 billion fact rows per year, so point-in-time balances come from transaction facts instead.
results.setup: 10 million accounts, one snapshot row per account per day
results.quote: If the bank has 10 million accounts, daily snapshots translate into approximately 3.65 billion fact rows per year.

results.claim: Most dimensional models end up with 5 to 15 or so dimensions; at or below the low end, suspect omitted dimensions.
results.setup: Rule of thumb for dimensional models in general
results.quote: In general, most dimensional models end up with between 5 and 15 or so dimensions.

results.claim: The core snapshot ends with six dimensions: month end date, account, household, branch, product, status.
results.setup: Bank monthly account snapshot, grain one row per account per month
results.quote: month end date, account, household, branch, product, and status

results.claim: The master account dimension in a big bank may approach 10 million members, which makes type 2 SCD on it unworkable, so product, branch, household and volatile attributes are moved out.
results.quote: the master account dimension in a big bank may approach 10 million members

results.claim: Example value-band report: 45,678 accounts in the 0-1,000 band totalling $10,222,543, and the report scans more than 90,000 account balances.
results.setup: Account balance snapshot, five bands (0-1,000 to 10,001 and up)
results.quote: Perhaps only the date dimension was constrained to the current month.

limits: Chapter says its schemas are not full-scale industry solutions and should not be viewed as complete.
Retail banking only; no performance measurements, all examples illustrative.
Point-in-time technique requires a complete and accurate transaction table; a late-arriving row forces sweeping forward and incrementing later balances and sequence numbers.
Point-in-time balances are invalid when the balance changes without transactions, e.g. brokerage valuations; use a snapshot instead.
Dated: Sybase IQ fact indexing was described as becoming standard in competing DBMSs as of 2002; modern columnar engines make this routine.
practices: Declare the grain first (one row per account per month), then triage for missing dimensions; fewer than about 5 suggests omissions (p.200).
Pull product and branch out of the account dimension into their own dimensions as smaller entry points and to limit type 2 SCD growth (p.200).
Check candidate extra dimensions: causal, multiple dates, degenerate, role-playing, status, audit, junk (p.201); they can be added later without changing grain.
Any descriptive attribute single-valued in the presence of the fact measurements is a candidate for an existing or new dimension (p.201).
Treat account balances as semi-additive: not additive across time, so average by dividing the balance sum by number of months (p.201).
Model status as a full dimension with decodes, groupings and reasons rather than a cryptic code in the fact table (p.202).
Build a household dimension and capture the account-household relationship in the fact table rather than type 2 on the account dimension (p.203).
Householding needs business rules and algorithms, often specialised matching products (p.203).
Use an account-to-customer bridge table with a weighting factor for multivalued customers; no bridge if the fact is at customer grain (p.204).
Split volatile browseable attributes (credit bureau, demographics, scores) into correlated-clump minidimensions keyed in the periodic snapshot; do not make each attribute its own (p.205).
Band minidimension attributes (income ranges, score ranges) and also store discrete values as facts for data mining and band checking, uniquely labelled (p.205-206).
For arbitrary value-band reports use a band definition table joined with >= and < joins to the fact; consider an index on the balance fact (p.206-207).

Use the transaction fact table with transaction sequence number, final flag and ending balance for point-in-time balances; select the max date key on or before the target date per account (p.208-209).
Key transaction fact on date, account and sequence number rather than time-of-day because sequence differences measure activity (p.209).
For heterogeneous products keep a core fact and product dimension with common facts, and a custom schema per line of business containing core plus special facts and attributes (p.210-211).
Custom product dimensions are row subsets of the core product dimension and reuse the same surrogate keys, keeping them conformed (p.211).
Where lines share table space, link an extended fact table to the core fact via a special join key and make the optimizer resolve core constraints first (p.213).
Use context-dependent outriggers for line-specific product attributes and account-specific attributes such as mortgage property details, via a view per product type (p.212).
With transaction-grained facts one core fact table suffices; use the core or custom product dimension depending on cross- or single-product analysis (p.214).

terms.definition: Checking a draft model for missing dimensions when it has too few.
A single physical dimension appearing several times in a fact table, each represented as a separate logical table with unique column names through views.
Business rules and algorithms to assign accounts to households.
A dimension where more than one value, such as several account holders, associates with a single fact row; handled with a bridge table.
Browseable and changeable attributes broken off into separate dimensions whose keys are in the fact table.
Table of band group, sort order, range name, lower and upper values joined to a fact by less-than and greater-than joins.
A core fact and product dimension with common facts, plus per-line-of-business schemas with specific facts and attributes.
Line-specific attributes in an extended-product outrigger reached by a snowflake key from the base product dimension.

code.snippet:
SELECT A.ACCTNUM, F.BALANCE
FROM FACT F, ACCOUNT A
WHERE F.ACCOUNT_KEY = A.ACCOUNT_KEY
AND F.DATE_KEY = (SELECT MAX(G.DATE_KEY) FROM FACT G WHERE G.ACCOUNT_KEY = F.ACCOUNT_KEY AND G.DATE_KEY IN (SELECT D.DATE_KEY FROM DATE D WHERE D.FULLDATE <= 'January 5, 2002'))
